newsitem.title: POLAND: NEW POLISH SECURITIES LAW TO ADAPT RULES TO OECD.
newsitem.headline: NEW POLISH SECURITIES LAW TO ADAPT RULES TO OECD.

text.p: The lower house of the Polish parliament started discussing late on Wednesday a bill on public trade that analysts said will help adjust the country's securities law to the norms of the European Union and OECD.
The lower house sent the bill to parliamentary committees and final passage is expected in this year's second quarter.

Analysts said the law would create a legal framework for the introduction of new instruments such as futures and options and help Polish brokerages develop by granting them the right to provide investment-bank-type services.

"Brokerages' rights are too low...and there will be pressure for them to transform into investment banks, which is important because such banks which form in Poland know the local economic reality better than Western banks with scores of experience," said Waldemar Gebus of Raiffeisen Capital & Investment.

Analysts said foreigners have sometimes been surprised to call their Polish broker to be told he or she was unauthorised to provide advice, while in coming months the same houses could start advising on public offerings and similar operations.

They said another advantage was that only banks, brokerages and insurance firms would be allowed to underwrite issues, unlike the current legislation which allows any firm or even an individual to insure an issue.
Analysts said that in addition to derivatives trade, which the bourse says could start in this year's second quarter, the law would permit investors short selling.
They said the law would also reduce some of the bureaucracy that has sometimes made the Polish market seem over-regulated.

Polish Securities Commission (KPW) head Jacek Socha has said that the bill would allow Polish companies to float up to 25 percent of shares abroad without the Securities Commission's permission, either directly or through depositary receipts.
After the year 2000, the firms would be allowed to float unlimited stock abroad without a permit.

Socha, whose KPW drafted the bulk of the bill, has said companies traded publicly for more than 36 months would no longer have to submit issue prospectuses of new share issues for Securities Commission approval, simplifying capital raises.
The bill would also let foreign brokerages open branches in Poland rather than having to register separate firms and would allow for the creation of close-ended investment funds.
It would also give Polish citizens the opportunity to buy shares on international markets.
Analysts said a good sign was the fact the bill sought to provide recognition of beneficial ownership rights.
Some foreigners have complained that a broker cannot buy stock on behalf of a client and then transfer the stock to him. Instead, investors such as fund managers need to set up mirrored accounts.

"(The law) should regulate so-called benefical owner and legal owner cases. It contains specific regulations allowing for the facilitating of the functioning of foreign entities on the Polish capital market," Socha wrote on Thursday in the financial daily Nowa Europa.

The bill is also expected to encourage the privatisation of the Warsaw Stock Exchange, so far acting as non-profit organisation largely controlled by the state treasury, by allowing bourse member securities houses to earmark up to 20 percent of profit for dividend.
